new_or_updated_candidate_findings.mechanism: Use tests of candidate dependence/clustering levels to diagnose and document the likely independent evaluation unit, but do not automatically use the same data to choose a finer variance model and then treat downstream confidence intervals, sequential stopping, or pass/fail gates as if the clustering level had been fixed ex ante. For decision-critical inference, pre-specify a defensible coarse unit, use an independently calibrated/split sample for level selection, or employ a selection-aware procedure; otherwise keep the diagnostic separate from the final inferential gate.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.evidence: MacKinnon, Nielsen and Webb's bottom-up score-variance procedure uses the intersection-union principle and determines a nested clustering level without inflating the family-wise rejection rate of the clustering tests themselves. But Section 3.5/6.4 explicitly separates that guarantee from coefficient inference: selecting fine versus coarse clustering by the test is pre-testing. In 400,000-replication simulations, pre-test confidence intervals slightly over-cover when the fine/no-clustering null is exactly true, then under-cover more than always-coarse intervals at intermediate coarse-correlation strength because Type-II errors select an interval that is too short. The undercoverage is more pronounced with a 0.05 pre-test than a 0.20 pre-test; larger N reduces the problematic region by raising selection power.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.quantitative: Final-paper experiment: 12 coarse clusters; 4,800 or 24,000 observations; 400,000 replications. Earlier working-paper figure C.5: N=5,000,G=10 and N=5,000,G=20 pre-test coverage falls to roughly 0.91-0.93 over intermediate dependence for the 0.05 selector before recovering; N=20,000,G=20 narrows that bad region. The final paper states fine/HC3 coverage rapidly falls below 0.90 once coarse dependence is present, while pre-test intervals still under-cover more than coarse CV3 intervals at intermediate dependence.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.scope: Nested one-dimensional clustering in linear regression, not a direct theorem for agent benchmarks. The transferable point is the separation between 'selection test has controlled error' and 'post-selection downstream inference remains valid'.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.uncertainty: Need a direct method for selection-aware sequential inference when the task/trajectory/step hierarchy itself is estimated from evaluation data. Sample splitting is safe conceptually but may waste scarce independent tasks.

new_or_updated_candidate_findings.mechanism: Before trusting asymptotic benchmark uncertainty or small apparent score deltas, compute diagnostics at the candidate independent-unit level: raw cluster count, effective cluster count, cluster-size imbalance, leverage/influence, and treatment/success-condition concentration. When clusters are few or heterogeneous, prefer a cluster-jackknife-aware restricted wild bootstrap (WCR-S-like resampling) or another validated small-cluster method over naive normal/t inference. Treat bootstrap validity itself as configuration-dependent rather than automatic.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.evidence: MacKinnon, Nielsen and Webb show conventional CV1 inference can fail badly even with many nominal clusters when leverage/size imbalance is strong. Their WCR-S bootstrap transforms restricted scores with a cluster-jackknife correction. In 400,000-replication experiments with 24 clusters, 9,600 observations and varying cluster imbalance or regressor dimension, WCR-S consistently improves on classic WCR-C and often performs extremely well. With clusters G from 12 to 84, WCR-S is the best method in the skewed-regressor design for every G and performs remarkably well for G>=30. At G=84, nominal 5% rejection was 4.97% for WCR-S versus 9.04% for CV1 and 7.15% for CV2; even CV3 was 5.49%. The authors recommend WCR-S as their single default bootstrap choice, while warning that extreme few-treated-cluster cases can still defeat bootstrap variants.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.quantitative: Representative null rejection at G=84: WCR-S 4.97%, CV3 5.49%, CV2 7.15%, CV1 9.04%. Simulations use 400,000 replications; the paper generally uses B=399 or 999 for simulation and recommends >=9,999 bootstrap draws in practice. An empirical example has CV3 SE 47% larger than CV1 despite 70 clusters, demonstrating raw G alone is not enough.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.scope: Linear regression cluster inference. For agent evaluation, the candidate mechanism is the diagnostic structure and cluster-level resampling principle, not literal use of WCR-S unless the score estimator fits its assumptions.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.uncertainty: Agent outcomes are often bounded, paired, multi-model, and adaptively sampled rather than OLS residuals. Need analogous bootstrap/e-process constructions for paired task-level score differences and sequential looks.

new_or_updated_candidate_findings.mechanism: Do not assume a single task-level cluster axis is sufficient when evaluation records can share dependence along multiple crossed dimensions. Explicitly map plausible dependence axes (for example task/task-family, generator or policy instance, judge/evaluator, environment seed/source) and test whether one-way clustering materially understates uncertainty. If multiple non-nested axes remain plausible, use a multi-way cluster-aware bootstrap/covariance construction or design the benchmark so one axis is randomized/blocked away.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.evidence: MacKinnon, Nielsen and Webb's multi-way clustering work shows that using a one-way CRVE when two-way clustering is present can cause extremely severe inference errors, especially at larger sample sizes; conventional t inference with multi-way CRVEs can also be unreliable when either dimension has few clusters, while appropriate wild bootstrap procedures are much more accurate in most simulated cases. A newer 2025 causal-function paper extends score-bootstrap logic to multi-way clustering and proves asymptotically valid uniform confidence bands; its simulations report better finite-sample size control with multi-way cross-fitting than full-sample pointwise inference.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.quantitative: Evidence here is primarily structural plus extensive simulation direction; exact 2025 Table 6.1 cells are not yet extracted. The older multi-way paper explicitly reports that one-way inference can be 'extremely severe' under true two-way dependence and that bootstrap gains are largest when at least one dimension has few clusters.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.scope: Crossed/multi-way dependence, distinct from nested step→trajectory→task dependence. Multi-way cluster bootstrap does not by itself solve optional stopping or a hierarchy chosen after seeing outcomes.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.uncertainty: Need agent-specific simulations with crossed task×judge or task×policy dependence and exact size/coverage comparisons against simple task clustering.

scoped_or_rejected_leads.lead: A clustering-level test that controls family-wise error makes downstream confidence intervals valid after choosing the cluster level on the same data.
scoped_or_rejected_leads.reason: Rejected. The clustering diagnostic's FWER and downstream post-selection inference are different guarantees. MacKinnon et al.'s simulations show Type-II selection errors can create substantial intermediate-region undercoverage.

scoped_or_rejected_leads.lead: Choose the finest cluster level that a 5% diagnostic fails to reject, because stricter testing is always safer.
scoped_or_rejected_leads.reason: Rejected. A lower-alpha pre-test makes fewer Type-I errors but more Type-II errors; the paper finds 0.05 pre-test intervals under-cover more severely than 0.20 pre-test intervals at intermediate dependence.

scoped_or_rejected_leads.lead: Raw number of clusters is an adequate reliability diagnostic.
scoped_or_rejected_leads.reason: Rejected. Cluster imbalance, leverage/influence, regressor concentration and treated-cluster count can dominate nominal G; an empirical example has a 47% CV3-vs-CV1 SE gap even with 70 clusters.

scoped_or_rejected_leads.lead: Wild cluster bootstrap is automatically trustworthy whenever clusters are few.
scoped_or_rejected_leads.reason: Rejected. WCR variants can under-reject severely with very few treated clusters, and unrestricted variants can badly over-reject; bootstrap configuration and balance diagnostics matter.

scoped_or_rejected_leads.lead: Once task-level clustering is used, additional crossed dependence axes can be ignored.
scoped_or_rejected_leads.reason: Rejected as a general rule. Multi-way clustering results show one-way methods can fail badly under crossed dependence. Whether an agent benchmark actually has such axes must be diagnosed rather than assumed.
